IMWDb, WatchPro and A Timely Perspective all say Hamilton supplied the Khaki Pilot Pioneer Aluminum for The Martian, worn by Jessica Chastain as Commander Lewis and by Kate Mara as Johanssen. The model came out in 2014, before the 2015 film, so the timing fits. The sources name the model only, not an exact reference.

Tom Selleck's Thomas Magnum is well documented wearing a Chronosport Sea Quartz 30 dive watch in the early seasons of Magnum, P.I., before he switched to the Rolex GMT-Master. Watches of Espionage, the card's cited source, and watch-in-film databases both record this.

It's well documented that Steve McQueen wore the blue-dial Heuer Monaco ref. 1133B, which has an automatic Calibre 11 movement, as Michael Delaney in Le Mans (1971). One of the watches used in the film was sold at a Phillips auction in 2020.

Steve McQueen wearing the Monaco in Le Mans (1971) is well documented: it was the blue Heuer Monaco ref. 1133B, sold under the Heuer name before the brand became TAG Heuer. The card's source is an unrelated Pedro Pascal article and gives no passages, but the sighting is real.
In GoldenEye (1995), Pierce Brosnan's Bond wears the Omega Seamaster Professional Diver 300M quartz, ref. 2541.80.00. This was Bond's first Omega, and both Omega's own history and IMWDb record it.

It's well documented that Andy Warhol wore a Cartier Tank. He is often quoted saying he wore it not to tell the time, and Tanks from his collection were sold in the 1988 Sotheby's estate auction. The card's linked source is a Vogue piece about Timothée Chalamet's Cartier necklace, so it doesn't support the sighting, but the sighting is real.

Sotheby's July 2026 Space Exploration auction sold a LeCoultre 'Shark Deep Sea' chronograph, ref. 2643, from the Buzz Aldrin Family Trust, taken directly from Aldrin's personal collection. GQ and Gear Patrol report the same lot, so his ownership of this watch is confirmed.

IMWDb and A Timely Perspective's 2015 coverage of Hamilton's work on the film both say Michael Peña's character, Rick Martinez, wears the Hamilton Khaki X-Wind Limited Edition in The Martian. Neither source names an exact reference number, which is why the card leaves it blank.

Rolex's US site lists the 126200-0001 (silver dial, Jubilee bracelet) at USD 8,350. That's roughly CHF 6.6k–7k, so it fits the budget, and the 36 mm size, 100 m water resistance and automatic movement match the request. The steel Datejust 36 is a classic everyday watch that specialists gladly recommend for a 15.7 cm wrist.

My searches didn't bring up this exact quartz reference, but the card links to the Davosa USA product page, and 40 mm, 200 m and about USD 838 fit the Ternos range. I found nothing that contradicts the card. It's a reasonable Swiss quartz diver with a ceramic bezel that works for the office within budget, but it's a niche choice: solar divers from Seiko or Citizen, or Certina's quartz DS Action, are arguably stronger picks for the money.

The TAG Heuer 6000 WH1111 is a well-regarded 90s Swiss quartz diver (ETA 955.112, 200 m) at about 38 mm, so it suits a 15.8 cm wrist for everyday wear. But $1,150 pre-owned is high when comparable examples list for about $600–900, and the budget allows stronger picks.

The Steinhart Ocean 44 is a solid Swiss automatic diver with 300 m water resistance and a 44 mm case, which suits a 19 cm wrist, and about USD 580 (around GBP 460) is within budget. It's a well-known value pick among enthusiasts, though its Submariner-style design won't appeal to everyone. My search confirmed the specs but not the exact reference number.

The Panthère Jumbo 130000C is a square-ish quartz watch that measures 29 x 40 mm. It doesn't have a 36 mm diameter, so the size on the card is wrong. The pre-owned price of about USD 3,200 is consistent with what dealers are asking.

Oris's own page and several dealers list reference 01 400 7790 4157-07 8 23 02PEB as the 43.5 mm Aquis Date Calibre 400, not 41.5 mm. That puts it outside the 40–43 mm range for this request, and the '41.5' in the model name is wrong too. The USD 4,300 retail price, the automatic Calibre 400 movement and the 300 m water resistance are correct.

The card calls the SRPL53 a King Turtle, but it's actually the compact PADI Special Edition 'Samurai'. It has an angular case, the 4R35 movement and a date-only dial, while the King Turtle is a bigger day-date model with a 4R36 movement. The price, 41.7 mm size, automatic movement and 200 m rating are all correct.

The card names the ceramic BR 03 Diver Black Matte (BR03A-D-BL-CE/SRB), but it gives the reference, source and USD 4,600 price of a different watch, the steel BR 03 Diver Black Steel (BR03A-D-BL-ST/SRB). The 42 mm case, automatic movement and 300 m rating are right, and either version would otherwise suit the request.

Citizen's global site still lists the AR5000-50E. It is an ultra-thin (about 3 mm) solar dress watch with a sapphire crystal and a Duratect-hardened steel case. That makes it a strong, distinctive office pick for a small 15.3 cm wrist, and at about USD 2,300 (current listings run USD 2,070–2,440) it sits within the EUR 2k–3k budget. Retailers list the case at 39 mm against the card's 38.3 mm, a minor difference that still fits the 35–39 mm range, and the 30 m water rating matches the listed 3 ATM.

TAG Heuer's own specs list the Carrera Year of the Tiger WBN2050.FC6506 at 41 mm, not 39 mm, so it's too big for the 35–39 mm range. The pre-owned price of USD 7,182 is also hard to believe for a Calibre 5 limited edition that retailed at about USD 3,750–3,950, which makes it poor value.

The facts check out: the 1523.2 is a vintage Hublot Classic quartz watch, 36 mm, in steel and 18k gold, and dealer prices of about $2.2k–2.9k (roughly €2.2k–2.8k) sit inside the budget. It works as a slim office watch with cult appeal, but a two-tone vintage piece on a rubber strap is a niche taste and an older quartz watch can be costly to service, so options like a Grand Seiko quartz or a Cartier Tank/Santos would be safer picks.

Every fact on the card checks out against Maurice Lacroix's US site: this reference is 42 mm and automatic, rated to 200 m, and retails at USD 2,950, which fits the EUR 2–3k budget. The Aikon is a well-regarded everyday sports watch with an integrated bracelet, and this set includes an extra rubber strap, so it's good value.

The facts check out: 38 mm, 150 m, automatic calibre 8802, and the price is plausible against the budget. But this discontinued two-tone version has a diamond-set dial and a burgundy leather strap, so it's dressy rather than resort wear; a steel Aqua Terra on a bracelet or rubber strap would suit the request better.

Omega's US site confirms reference 220.10.38.20.09.001: a 38 mm Aqua Terra Shades in steel on a steel bracelet, with the automatic calibre 8800, rated to 150 m and priced at $7,400. A retailer listing confirms the Sandstone dial. In francs that comes to about CHF 6k, so it fits the budget, and it's a strong everyday pick for a 15.7 cm wrist.

The facts check out: the L3.689.4.03.6 is a 41 mm blue HydroConquest with a quartz movement (L115), 300 m water resistance and a 10.2 mm case, and USD 681 pre-owned is about £540, inside the budget. It's a slim Swiss diver from a respected brand with a sapphire crystal and a bracelet, so it works well for office wear and is a strong pick for this request.

The Orient Kamasu RA-AA0006L19B is a well-known value pick among enthusiasts. It has a 41.8 mm case, 200 m water resistance, an in-house automatic movement and a sapphire crystal, and the approximate price of about USD 233 fits easily within the GBP 500 budget.

The card says GBP 3,100 confirmed retail, but its own source (the S301 black-dial bracelet page, s301-bk-br) lists £3,500 and marks the model as retired from Bremont's catalogue. £3,100 is the price of the rubber-strap version (S301-BK-R-S). The S301/BK leather-strap reference had an RRP of £2,950. The 40 mm case, automatic movement and 300 m rating are correct, and the watch suits a resort request.

The facts check out: Breitling lists ref. A37330531A1A1 as a 36 mm steel automatic (caliber B37) with a mother-of-pearl dial and 100 m water resistance. A pre-owned price of USD 7,500 is believable against a USD 11,800 retail price, since this version has a diamond bezel. It fits the request, but it's a discontinued, diamond-set dress-jewelry piece at the top of the budget, and diamond Breitlings lose value fast. A watch specialist would more likely suggest a simpler everyday sports watch such as a Tudor Black Bay 36 or an Omega Aqua Terra 38.

The 40 mm case, BE-92AE automatic chronometer movement and 100 m water resistance all match Bremont's own spec page, and it's a pleasant everyday pilot watch. But Bremont has retired the model, and its last retail price (£3,450) was above this budget, so the approximate USD 2,792 is really a second-hand price. At EUR 2k–3k there are stronger picks, like a Sinn 556 or a Longines Spirit, which have better movements and hold their value better.

Chanel lists reference H5699 as the J12 Caliber 12.2 in white ceramic with a 33 mm case. It is not the 38 mm Calibre 12.1. The USD 7,950 price belongs to that 33 mm watch, and the 38 mm Calibre 12.1 (H5697) sells for USD 8,350. So the model, case size and movement on the card are all wrong.

The facts check out: reference 220.20.38.20.02.001 is the 38 mm steel and Sedna gold Aqua Terra with a silver dial, the automatic calibre 8800 and 150 m water resistance. USD 11,207 matches current pre-owned listings (about USD 12,000–13,200) and works out to roughly CHF 9k, which fits the budget. It's a polished, water-ready sports-dress watch that suits resort wear and a 15.1 cm wrist.

The facts check out: L3.689.4.59.2 is the 41 mm quartz HydroConquest with a black dial, red bezel and rubber strap, rated to 300 m, and about USD 963 pre-owned (roughly GBP 760) fits the budget. It's a solid Swiss quartz diver, but the red bezel and rubber strap are sporty for the office, so a black or blue version on the steel bracelet would suit the request better.

The facts check out: the L3.379.4 is a 36 mm Longines Conquest with an L538 quartz chronograph movement, so it suits the wrist and the budget. But it's an older, discontinued midsize piece, and USD 1,364 pre-owned is more than its last retail price of about $1,225. Newer quartz watches at this budget are better value.

The card calls this the max bill Quartz 34mm, but ref. 041/4465.04 is the 38 mm max bill Quartz with a black dial and the J645.33 movement, so the model name is wrong. The 38 mm size, 30 m water resistance and roughly USD 1,030 retail price are right, and the watch itself would be a strong pick for this request.

The card lists a 40 mm case, but the source page and Selfridges both give 42 mm for the I00702 Grafton. That is also outside the 37–40 mm range requested. Even apart from that, Ingersoll is a fashion-oriented brand and this busy multi-function dial is a weak office pick.

The specs are correct: Zenith's Elite 670 automatic movement in a 36 mm steel case rated to 100 m, and it fits within the budget. But the starry, ladies-oriented dial is a niche style for an everyday watch. And USD 7,649 is near the top of what dealers ask (similar pieces are listed at about USD 5.2k–6.4k), so better-value all-rounders fit this request.

The facts check out: it's 42 mm, runs on the H-31 automatic chronograph movement, is rated to 100 m, and USD 2,645 matches authorized dealer pricing. It fits the budget and the size range, but the busy racing-style design makes it a polarizing everyday watch, and the Hamilton Intra-Matic Chronograph or a Longines would be a cleaner, more versatile pick.

The 81925 is a vintage steel quartz Santos Ronde/Vendôme. That family (refs 8191, 8192, 81925) comes in about 27, 30 and 33 mm, not 38 mm, so the 38 mm on the card is almost certainly wrong. That would also put the watch below the 35–39 mm range the request asks for.

The card's facts hold up: Bulova's own listings show the 96B322 Devil Diver at 44 mm, automatic and 200 m, and about USD 488 is a believable discounted price within the GBP 500 budget. It's a fair sporty diver with a sapphire crystal, but its basic Miyota 821D movement makes it weaker value than divers like the Orient Kamasu or Seiko and Citizen automatic divers.

The water resistance on the card is wrong. Every launch source (Time Bum, Worn & Wound, WristReview) lists the C60 Apex Limited Edition at 300 m, not 600 m. I also couldn't confirm the USD 4,644 price: it launched in 2019 at £3,495 (US$3,990–4,243), and with only 100 pieces made it is now likely sold out and only available pre-owned.

The card's facts are right: the IW658602 is a 37 mm steel case with a diamond bezel, IWC's own automatic calibre 32111 and 50 m water resistance. But USD 11,373 pre-owned is more than discounted new ones cost (about USD 10,000–10,900, against USD 12,100 retail), and a dressy diamond-bezel watch on a calfskin strap is a weak choice for resort wear.

Borealis's own specs confirm a 38 mm case, a Miyota 9039 automatic and 300 m water resistance. Its listed price runs from USD 350 (sale) to USD 495, so the approximate USD 375 is realistic and well within GBP 500. A compact, well-made microbrand diver with sapphire crystal and a ceramic bezel is a strong pick for travel on a 16.5 cm wrist.

All the card's facts check out on Grand Seiko's own site: titanium 62GS case, 38 mm, Hi-Beat automatic 9S85 movement, 100 m water resistance, USD 7,900 retail. That price comes to about CHF 6.3k, inside the budget, and the watch is a strong everyday pick for a 15.7 cm wrist, though some buyers may find the pink 'Sakura-Kakushi' dial niche.

The facts check out: ref. 568.CM.1470.CM is the 38 mm black ceramic Black Magic on a ceramic bracelet, with the automatic HUB1110, 50 m water resistance and pre-owned prices around USD 11.1–11.3k, which is within CHF 9–10k. It suits a resort wrist, but a Sellita-based Hublot is weak value at this price, and an enthusiast would usually suggest stronger picks first.

I didn't run a search. From what I know of this model, the facts look right: the Boldr Venture is a 38 mm automatic with 200 m water resistance, and PLN 1320 is about £260, well within budget. Boldr is a well-liked microbrand and this is a tough, versatile field watch. It's a solid travel companion, but it has no second time-zone (GMT) hand, so an affordable automatic GMT would suit a travel request better.

Every fact on the card checks out against Omega's official US page. The reference is the 38 mm steel Summer Blue Aqua Terra on a bracelet, with the automatic Omega 8800, 150 m water resistance and a USD 7,800 retail price. At 38 mm it suits a 15.7 cm wrist, and it's a classic everyday watch that sits within the CHF 6k–7k budget.

The facts check out: the B77346 Callisto has a 34.4 mm case with Breitling's cal. 77 quartz movement, and about USD 2,200 pre-owned matches current listings. It's a sporty, dated two-tone Windrider model from the early 2000s, though, and a specialist would probably suggest a stronger office quartz for this budget, such as a Grand Seiko 9F.

The 36 mm size, quartz L420 movement, 30 m water resistance, reference and price of about USD 1,350–1,400 all check out, and it fits a 15.8 cm wrist. But this ultra-thin dress watch with Roman numerals is delicate for daily wear, and a sportier quartz like the Longines Conquest would suit 'everyday' better. The card's model name also mixes two separate lines: it is officially just 'La Grande Classique de Longines', and 'Présence' is a different collection, though some sellers use the combined name.

The Cartier Ronde Solo W6700255 is a steel 36 mm quartz watch from a respected maker. It fits a 15.8 cm wrist well and suits everyday wear. About USD 1,900 pre-owned is a fair dealer price and sits inside the budget, so a specialist would gladly recommend it for a classic quartz pick.

The Citizen Tsuyosa NJ0150-81E is a well-liked automatic. It has a 40 mm steel case on an integrated bracelet, 50 m water resistance and a Miyota 8210 movement, and it looks smart enough for the office. At about EUR 299 it fits well within a CHF 500 budget and is a sensible size for a 16.6 cm wrist, at the top of the 37–40 mm range.

The Santos Medium WSSA0010 (35.1 mm, cal. 1847 MC automatic, 100 m, steel QuickSwitch bracelet) is an iconic everyday watch that sits well on a 15.7 cm wrist. Sources list its US retail anywhere from $7,250 to $8,400, so the card's figure is plausible, and it is close to the CHF 6k–7k budget.

The facts check out: 42 mm steel case, Sellita SW200-1 automatic, 200 m water resistance, and the approximate price matches a list price of about CHF 2,250 before VAT. Eterna is a real Swiss heritage brand and the KonTiki suits everyday wear, but it uses a basic Sellita movement, sells for much less on the grey and secondary market, and holds its value poorly, so stronger picks exist at EUR 2–3k.

The size, movement and water resistance are right: a 40 mm Sellita SW200 automatic rated to 50 m. But Baume & Mercier's own page lists the 10214 as a discontinued 'Heritage' piece that is no longer available, so a 'confirmed retail' price of USD 2900 is wrong. Even at that price, a basic SW200 dress watch is weak value in this budget.

The card gets the water resistance wrong. Laco's official page and dealer listings rate this watch to 20 ATM (200 m), not 100 m. The price (USD 2,220), the 43 mm case and the automatic movement (Laco 330, based on the Sellita SW330) are all correct, and the watch otherwise suits the request well.

The specs check out: 41 mm, quartz (L157), 300 m water resistance, sapphire crystal and a steel bracelet, so it fits the size, movement and water-resistance asks. The UK list price is £850 (often about £750 discounted), which is within the £500–1k budget. It's a sporty Swiss quartz from a respected brand that also suits the office. The card's approximate USD 781 sits below the US list price of $900 but within the real market, where dealers sell it for about $720.

I couldn't find a 'Flygraf Pilot M1 GMT' or the reference YFLY22-GMT-BMS anywhere. The real Flygraf Pilot M1 (ref. YFLY2020-AMS) has no GMT function and is 39 mm with 300 m water resistance, so the card's model, reference, 40 mm size and 100 m rating don't match a real watch.

The facts check out: the CAF7111.BA0803 has a 41 mm case, 300 m water resistance and TAG's Calibre S electro-mechanical quartz movement, and USD 920 pre-owned is about GBP 730, which fits the budget. It's a discontinued model, though, and servicing the Calibre S can be tricky. The busy regatta dial is also more sporty than office-friendly, so a cleaner quartz or solar diver would suit the request better.

The card calls R32150168 the 'Captain Cook High-Tech Ceramic Diver', but Rado's own page (the card's source) lists it as the Captain Cook High-Tech Ceramic Skeleton, with the skeletonised R808 movement. The 43 mm case, automatic movement and 300 m water resistance are correct. I couldn't confirm the EUR 4,500 price because Rado lists it at CHF 3,950 and USD 4,700, so I haven't marked the price as wrong.

Laco lists reference 862103 as a discontinued model at USD 410. The USD 460 retail price belongs to the current successor, 862103.2. The card also shortens the model name, which is officially 'Aachen Blaue Stunde 39'. The 39 mm size, Miyota 82S0 automatic movement and 50 m water resistance are correct, and the watch would otherwise suit a CHF 500 office budget.

The facts check out against Eberhard's own site: a 43 mm automatic diver rated to 300 m, and the reference matches. At about GBP 3.2k it's within budget and suits a resort request, but 43 mm is the top of the range for this wrist, and full retail is steep when pre-owned ones sell for around $2.5k and a Tudor Pelagos or Oris Aquis costs about the same.

The facts check out. The SSJ003J1 is a 39 mm steel Astron GPS Solar with the 3X22 solar movement, and $1,604 is a fair pre-owned dealer price that fits the budget. Its 46.2 mm lug-to-lug suits a 15.8 cm wrist, which makes it a strong everyday solar pick. The card lists water resistance as unknown, but Seiko rates it to 100 m, which is a bonus.

Seiko's own page and a dealer listing both confirm the SSK023 at USD 450 retail, with a 39.4 mm case, the 4R34 automatic GMT movement and 100 m water resistance. It's a real GMT at a size that fits a 16.5 cm wrist and well under the £500 budget (UK dealers list it at around £410), so it's an excellent travel pick for the money.

Timex's own site confirms the facts: TW3A01600 is a 44 mm steel diver with a Miyota 8215 automatic and 200 m water resistance, listed at USD 499 (about £390, so within budget). It's a decent diver with sapphire, a ceramic bezel and a helium valve, but the 44 mm × 15.5 mm case is big for a 19 cm wrist, and the basic Miyota 8215 makes the value weaker than rivals like the Orient Kamasu or Seiko Prospex divers.

Reference 8086-4 is the 41 mm LZ129 Hindenburg Solar chronograph with a Seiko VR42A solar quartz movement, and the card's own source points to that solar model. The 40 mm automatic at EUR 299 is reference 8056-4. Even with the right reference, this 50 m fashion-leaning dress watch is a weak travel pick against a 100 m request.

The facts check out: 40 mm, Seiko NH35A automatic, 100 m, sapphire crystal, ref 1221505C. The official €485 price (about USD 551, CHF 455) is within budget. It's a well-regarded Italian microbrand, and this dressy integrated-bracelet piece suits the office well and is good value at this budget, though 40 mm sits at the top of the size range for a 16.6 cm wrist.

The facts check out: the 36 mm steel Defy Midnight Borealis has a diamond bezel, the automatic Elite calibre and 100 m water resistance, which suits a 15.1 cm wrist and resort wear. But USD 11,212 is poor value when Chrono24 has a 2026 example listed for about USD 6,700, and the gem-set bezel makes it a narrower pick than other options in this budget.

This is a good pick for this request: an in-house automatic YEMA2000 pilot watch under budget, which suits travel. But the card gets two facts wrong. The official Yema store and other retailers list the Flygraf Pilot M1 at 39 mm and 300 m water resistance, not the 40 mm and 100 m on the card. I also couldn't confirm that reference YFLY2020-C exists; the references I found are YFLY2020-AMS and -ACVS.

Grand Seiko's own site lists the SBGX261 at USD 2,700, and it is a 37 mm 9F quartz watch with 100 m water resistance, so every fact on the card checks out. A watch specialist would gladly pick it for this budget, wrist and office use: the 9F movement is one of the best quartz calibres made, and the Heritage design is restrained and very well finished.

Omega's own spec sheet and WatchBase confirm the facts: ref. 2502.34.00 is the 42.2 mm steel Aqua Terra on a bracelet, with the self-winding Co-Axial calibre 2500. Its sporty but dressy style and 150 m water resistance suit a resort trip. The USD 4,000 dealer price is about GBP 3,150, which is within budget, though Chrono24 listings run about $2,900–3,700, so the card's price is at the high end.

The facts check out: the 8926OB is a 40 mm Submariner homage with an NH35A automatic movement, 200 m water resistance, and a street price of about USD 100–135. But Invicta is widely seen as a mall brand, and this generic homage is a weak pick for an office watch when the same budget gets an Orient Bambino, Seiko 5 Sports, Orient Kamasu or Tissot PRX.

The facts on the card check out. The SRPH33 is a 5 Sports Field watch that lists at $350 on Seiko's US site, with a 39.4 mm case, the 4R36 automatic movement and 100 m water resistance. It's a well-sized, tough field watch that costs well under the £500 budget and suits travel, so a specialist would happily recommend it at this price.

Every fact on the card checks out. Grand Seiko's site lists the SBGH343 at USD 7,900, with a 38 mm titanium case, the 9S85 Hi-Beat automatic movement and 100 m water resistance. This light, well-finished everyday sports watch suits a 15.7 cm wrist, and the price falls roughly inside the CHF 6–7k budget.

The facts hold up: TAG Heuer's own page lists WAR1113.FC6392 as a 39 mm Swiss quartz Carrera Special Edition in black PVD steel (the card's 'Lady' name is the dealer's), and the price fits the budget. But it's a discontinued quartz Carrera with a fairly loud black-PVD look, and 39 mm is at the top of this wrist's range, so for an office watch at this budget there are better-value choices.

The facts check out: Omega lists ref. 1552.30.00 as a 35.5 mm steel case with the thermocompensated quartz perpetual calendar cal. 1680, and a dealer listing confirms 50 m water resistance. It's a high-quality quartz watch that suits a 15.8 cm wrist for daily wear, and USD 1,938 pre-owned fits the budget, though one UK dealer sold one for £1,295, so this price is on the high side.

Omega's own spec sheet confirms the card: ref. 1252.30.00 is a 35.5 mm Constellation in steel and yellow gold with the cal. 1680 thermocompensated quartz perpetual calendar and 50 m water resistance. At about USD 2.3k pre-owned it's within the EUR 2–3k budget, in line with current Chrono24 listings, and it's a refined office watch that suits a small wrist, though the two-tone 2000s look won't appeal to everyone.

The card calls this watch a "Pro Diver GMT", but the 9404 is a plain three-hand automatic Pro Diver (NH35A movement, white dial, coke bezel) with no GMT hand. That error matters for a travel request. The 40 mm case, automatic movement and 200 m water resistance are correct, and the roughly USD 91 price fits the street price (about $107 on Amazon), though Invicta itself is a weak brand pick for an enthusiast site.

The card calls this watch the 'Conquest 38', but L3.830.4.52.6 is the 41 mm Conquest, as Longines' own page and several dealers show. The other facts check out: 41 mm, L888 automatic, 100 m, USD 2,400 retail. The watch itself would be a strong pick for this request.

The facts check out: TW2U29500 is the M79 Automatic, 40 mm, Miyota automatic, 50 m, and it launched at USD 279 (now listed at USD 289). It's a fun budget pick, but this sporty 1970s diver look with a rotating bezel, 14.5 mm thick case and acrylic crystal doesn't suit an office very well, and other watches under CHF 500 are dressier and better made.

The card's facts check out: GL0088 is a Combat Sub 42 with a 42 mm case, a Swiss automatic movement (GL224, a Sellita-based calibre) and 200 m water resistance. Glycine's own US store sells Combat Sub 42 models for about USD 515–540, which is roughly £430 and inside the £500 budget. A Swiss automatic diver with a sapphire crystal and a screw-down crown is a strong pick for this sport request.

The model name is wrong. The PY010C is sold as the Wave Master 300M (300 m water resistance, NH35A movement, 42 mm case, USD 289), not the "Wave Master 200M". The rest of the card is right, and the watch would otherwise be a strong-value diver within budget.

The size (41 mm), quartz L115 movement, 300 m water resistance and reference all check out. A pre-owned price of about USD 963 (roughly £760) is within budget, and a quartz Swiss diver with a sapphire crystal on a steel bracelet works well for the office.

Ref. 140.019.5 is a small quartz Reverso in steel and gold from around 2000, and its case is about 22 x 32 mm, not 37 mm. It is far too small for the 35–39 mm range, even though the quartz movement and the roughly USD 2.7k–4k pre-owned price are plausible.

The Orient Star Elegant Classic RE-AU0002S is a well-regarded automatic dress watch with a 38.5 mm case, power reserve indicator and 50 m water resistance. It suits office wear and fits the wrist size. At about USD 497 it fits the CHF 500 budget and offers strong value at this price.

The SBGX295 has a white dial on a black crocodile strap, not a black dial. Its retail price is also well above the card's figure: ¥363,000 in Japan, about SGD 2,775 at a Singapore dealer, and likely about USD 2,700–2,900 in the US (an estimate). The size (37 mm), 9F62 quartz movement and 100 m water resistance are correct.

FC-335MC4P6 is the Classics Heart Beat Moonphase Date, not a 'Manufacture' model. Its FC-335 movement is built on a Sellita SW200 base, not made in-house. Frederique Constant and retailers list the case as 40 mm, not 40.5 mm, which is also just under the requested 40–43 mm.

Every fact on the card is correct: 41 mm, Swiss quartz (L157), 300 m, silver dial on a leather strap. A Longines Conquest with a dressy silver dial is a strong office watch that can also handle real water use. The pre-owned price of about USD 911 (roughly GBP 720) is within budget and in line with dealer listings, though it sits a little above the old USD 825 retail.

All the card's facts check out: reference L3.659.4.76.5 is the 41 mm steel Conquest quartz with a silver dial, brown leather strap, sapphire crystal and 300 m water resistance. At about USD 729 pre-owned (roughly GBP 580) it fits the budget, and it suits the office while still being a capable 300 m sports watch.

Every fact on the card checks out: 126200-0023 is the steel Datejust 36 with the mint green dial and Jubilee bracelet, a 36 mm case, the automatic calibre 3235 and 100 m water resistance. It's a classic, versatile size for a 15.1 cm wrist and the green dial suits a resort brief. The pre-owned price of about USD 11.2k (roughly CHF 9k) is in line with dealer listings and within budget, though it sits above the USD 8,350 retail price.

The card's details are mixed up. Herbelin's 1645 references are the automatic Cap Camarat with a Sellita SW200 movement, rated to 100 m. The quartz 40.5 mm Cap Camarat is reference 12245, costs about €600 and is also rated to 100 m, so neither version reaches the 200 m on the card, and I found no 'Diver Quartz 1645/N14'.

The card's facts are right: USD 5,200 retail, 42 mm, Breitling 17 automatic, 300 m. The UK price of £3,950 fits the budget, and the steel bracelet and 300 m rating suit resort wear. But the Avenger's chunky aviation look and basic Sellita-based calibre with 38 hours of power reserve make it a so-so pick; a Breitling Superocean, Tudor Pelagos or pre-owned Omega Aqua Terra would suit a resort request better.

The I.N.O.X. Chrono is a well-built Swiss quartz watch, 43 mm with 200 m water resistance, and the price fits the budget. I couldn't confirm reference 241987 or its USD 694 price; sister steel references list at USD 800, so the approximate figure is plausible. As an office watch, though, its chunky, rugged look is less suitable than dressier 200 m quartz or solar options such as a Seiko Prospex solar, Citizen Promaster or Tissot Seastar.

Baltic's official page confirms the HMS 002 Silver: 38 mm, Miyota 8315 automatic, 50 m water resistance, €385 (about CHF 360, so within budget). This dressy step-case design from a respected microbrand is a strong office pick for a 16.6 cm wrist at this price.

The Certina DS Action Diver is a real ISO 6425 diver at 43 mm, with the Powermatic 80 automatic movement (80-hour power reserve) and 300 m water resistance. The approximate USD 568 is in line with grey-market prices of about USD 550 (list price USD 895), which keeps it within the GBP 500 budget. Specialists commonly recommend it at this price.

The facts check out: it's 39 mm, hand-wound with the in-house Kaliber 1 movement, rated to 50 m, and authorized dealers sell it for USD 11,900, which lands roughly within the CHF 9k–10k budget. It's an excellent independent watch, but its fully polished case and unusual hour display make it a dress piece, so it's a less natural fit for a resort watch than a sportier option.

Habring2's official specs give the Chrono-Felix 30 m of water resistance, not the 50 m on the card. That is also below the request's 50 m minimum for resort wear. The 38.5 mm case and hand-wound A11C monopusher movement are correct.

Every fact on the card is right: ref. 782 has a 42 mm case, NOMOS's own neomatik automatic movement and 300 m water resistance, and US retail is $5,050. That price comes to roughly £3,800–4,000, inside the budget. With its sporty steel bracelet, blue dial and real water resistance, it's a strong, distinctive choice for a resort watch.

The card's facts are right: this reference is the 36 mm quartz (VHP) Conquest with a diamond bezel and mother-of-pearl dial, and USD 3,198 fits the budget. But it's a flashy ladies' version, and a plain steel Conquest VHP without diamonds would suit office wear better. It's also poor value pre-owned, since new grey-market prices are around the same.

The facts look right: Q1558421 is the 39 mm automatic Master Calendar with a meteorite dial and 50 m water resistance, and about USD 11.5k pre-owned is roughly CHF 9.2k, which is within budget. But a dressy triple-calendar moonphase on a leather strap is a poor fit for resort wear near water, where a specialist would suggest a sportier, water-friendly piece instead.

The case size on the card is wrong. Oris's own spec pages and several dealer listings give the BC3 Day Date ref. 7500 as 40 mm, not 38 mm. Only a fan site about watches seen in films says 38 mm. The card also lists water resistance as unknown, but Oris rates it at 5 bar (50 m), which is below the 100 m the visitor asked for. It also has no travel feature such as a GMT hand.

Ball's own site confirms the facts: 41.5 mm, 300 m, in-house automatic COSC caliber RRM7309-C, and US$3,999 retail, which is about £3.1–3.2k and inside the budget. A blue sport diver with tritium tubes and a sapphire bezel suits a resort brief well and is good value for an enthusiast.

The Citizen Promaster NY0040 is a classic, well-liked budget automatic dive watch. It has a 42 mm case, an in-house Miyota 8203-family automatic movement and 200 m of water resistance, so it fits the sport brief. At about USD 244 it sits well inside the GBP 500 budget, and the card's facts match the real watch.

The card's facts are right: 42 mm, Miyota 8215 automatic, 300 m, and about £199–299 at UK dealers, so it fits the budget. But it's a department-store brand with a basic movement, the model has been discontinued, and enthusiasts would rather get an Orient Kamasu, a Seiko 5 Sports or a microbrand diver for this money.

The card says 100 m water resistance, but Grand Seiko's official spec sheet lists the SLGW003 as only splash resistant (some dealers say 30 m). That is far below the 50 m minimum and doesn't work for a resort watch. It is also a thin, dressy titanium watch on a crocodile strap, which suits resort wear poorly.

The card's facts check out: 40 mm case, automatic Valjoux 7750 chronograph, 100 m water resistance, and Damasko's own price of about €2,868, which fits the €2k–3k budget. It's a tough, well-made 40 mm German chronograph that suits an 18.5 cm wrist for daily wear, though at 13.8 mm it's fairly thick.

The Amphibia 120512 is a well-loved automatic diver with 200 m water resistance and a strong price at about USD 155–180. Sources list it as 39–40 mm without the crown, so the size holds up. But at about 15 mm thick, with an acrylic crystal and a rubber strap, it's a casual tool watch, and the budget leaves room for dressier office picks like an Orient Bambino or a Seiko Presage.

The facts on the card are right: it lists for USD 629 and has a 40 mm case, an automatic Miyota 9075 'true' GMT movement and 300 m water resistance. A true GMT that fits this wrist is a strong travel pick, but two things need checking: UK import VAT could push the landed cost past GBP 500, and some retailers show this limited edition as sold out.

The Seiko 5 Sports is a solid automatic at a good price, and it fits the budget and the 37–40 mm range (the newer compact SRPK models are about 39.4 mm). But the card names a whole product line with no reference, and its sporty diver look is not ideal for the office. A dressier automatic like the Orient Bambino or a Seiko Presage would suit the request better.

The facts check out: Omega's own page confirms the reference is a 35 mm steel case with the quartz calibre 1532, a white Supernova dial with diamond indexes, and a white rubber strap. Chrono24 lists 100 m water resistance, and USD 1,938 pre-owned is a plausible dealer price. It fits the request, but this is a women's diamond-dial piece on white rubber, which is a niche style for everyday wear. A plain-dial Constellation quartz on a bracelet would suit most buyers better.

The IWC Da Vinci SL quartz chronograph (ref. 3728, 37 mm, steel) is a real piece of IWC history, and its slim, classic look suits a 15.3 cm wrist in the office. At about USD 2,300 pre-owned it fits the EUR 2–3k budget, in line with current dealer listings of roughly USD 2,450–3,300.

The 42 mm case, automatic chronometer movement (RR1201-C), 100 m water resistance and reference all check out. The approximate USD 2,681 is below the USD 3,749–3,899 list price, but it matches real discounted and grey-market prices of about USD 2,800, so it's realistic for the EUR 2–3k budget. It's a well-respected tool GMT with tritium lume that works well every day, though it's a bit thick at 13.85 mm.
